newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TELECOMS-NZ Telecom to take on Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TELECOMS-NZ Telecom to take on Australia.

text.p: Telecom Corp of New Zealand Ltd says it is shaping up to become a major player in the Australian telecommunications market post-deregulation in mid-1997.

Telecom, which is now New Zealand's largest company and Australasia's fifth or sixth largest by market capitalisation, also sees the eventual creation of a single Australia/New Zealand telecommunications market.
"We see ourselves as an influential and important long term player in Australia," Telecom's chairman Peter Shirtcliffe told Reuters in a recent interview.
Shirtcliffe said he would not be specific about how Telecom would dive into the Australian market, but said it looked forward to deregulation from July 1 next year.
"We will be long term stakeholders in the Australian telecommunications environment," he said.
Shirtcliffe sees parallels between the single Trans-Tasman aviation market agreed this month and a potential single telecommunications market.
"The regulatory borders are crumbling. Ultimately there will be some parallels in telecoms."
Air New Zealand Ltd agreed this month to buy half of Ansett Australia, ensuring its full scale participation in the Australian domestic market.
The Australia-New Zealand Closer Economic Relations Trade Agreement (ANZCERTA) agreement established in the early 1980s would be the mechanism to reduce these barriers.
"ANZCERTA -- Those arrangements are now spilling over into the services area. A single market, that's the way we're heading over time."
Analysts said such an agreement would increase the likelihood of an eventual alliance between Telecom and either the state-owned Telstra Corp and the privately-held Optus Communications.

"If Telecom's talking about a single market and it wants a significant stake in Australia then ultimately its going to have to link up with Optus or Telstra," said HSBC James Capel analyst Adam Spowers.
Shirtcliffe said Telecom had already looked at an Optus stake, expressing an interest when Mayne Nickless Ltd said it may sell its 25 percent stake by a trade sale.
Mayne eventually decided in July to sell its Optus shares to its own shareholders and through Optus' float later this year.
Mayne said it could not identify a suitable trade buyer in discussions with Optus' other major shareholders, BellSouth Corp and Cable and Wireless, who each have 24.5 percent stakes.
Telecom's rejection was widely seen as dictated by BellSouth and Cable and Wireless, who were seen as reluctant to bring another big telecoms company onto the register.
Telstra is seen as the other potential Telecom partner, particularly if the latter is treated as a local company under any single market plan.

Until now the Australian government has said it would limit single foreign investors to a five percent stake in Telstra if, as planned, a third of it is privatised. Foreigners would be limited to about 12 percent of Telstra in total under the one-third sale plan.

But analysts said the draft Telstra sale bill, which has yet to be tabled, specifies New Zealand companies be treated differently, raising the prospect of Telecom as Telstra's foreign strategic stakeholder.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
